# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 19 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 19

---

1 But wrath without mercy came upon the ungodly to the very end; for God foreknew what they would yet do —

2 how, having themselves permitted the departure and sent the Israelites forth with urgency, they would repent and pursue them.

3 For while they were still engaged in mourning and lamenting at the graves of the dead, they conceived another foolish plan, and pursued as fugitives those whom they had driven out with entreaties.

4 For the fate they deserved was drawing them to this end, and it made them forget what had happened, so that they might fill up the punishment still lacking in their torments.

5 Thus your people might journey through the water by a miraculous way, while they themselves met a strange death.

6 For the whole of creation, in its proper order, was being fashioned anew, serving your distinct commands, so that your children might be kept unharmed.

7 The cloud was seen overshadowing the camp, and dry land appeared where water had been before; out of the Red Sea an unobstructed road, and a grassy plain out of the raging flood —

8 and through it the whole nation passed, protected by your hand, beholding your marvelous wonders.

9 For they grazed like horses, and they leaped about like lambs, praising you, O Lord, who had delivered them.

10 For they still remembered what had happened in their sojourn: how the land brought forth gnats instead of cattle, and the river swarmed with frogs instead of fish.

11 But afterward they also saw a new kind of bird, when, led on by craving, they demanded delicacies of food,

12 for quails came up from the sea for their nourishment.

13 And the punishments came upon the sinners not without prior signs given through the violence of thunder; for they suffered justly in keeping with their own wickedness, since they had shown a more bitter hatred toward strangers.

14 For some had merely refused to receive strangers they had never known, but these others had enslaved guests who were their benefactors.

15 And not only this; but there will be a particular accounting for those others, since they received strangers with hostility — whereas the Sodomites had treated as enemies those who came to them as guests.

16 But these Egyptians, after welcoming the Israelites with celebrations and granting them equal rights, later afflicted them with terrible hardships.

17 And they were struck with blindness, as also those at the door of the righteous man — when each of them, wrapped in impenetrable darkness, searched for the passage through his own doorway.

18 For the elements rearranged themselves with one another, just as on a harp the notes vary the character of the melody while the rhythm remains the same throughout; and this is what may be accurately inferred from the observation of what took place.

19 For land creatures became water creatures, and swimming creatures transferred themselves to dry land.

20 Fire maintained its own power in the water, and water forgot its own quenching nature.

21 On the other hand, flames did not scorch the flesh of perishable creatures moving about among them, nor did they melt the easily-melted, ice-like kind of heavenly nourishment.

22 For in all things, O Lord, you magnified and glorified your people, and did not fail to assist them at every time and place.

---

**Council Notes:**

Chapter 19 is the finale of the Wisdom of Solomon. It returns to the Red Sea to bring the Egypt/Israel antithesis to its conclusion, then draws a philosophical inference about creation's malleability (vv. 18–21) before the doxological close (v. 22).

V. 6: "fashioned anew" — EMET's "fashioned anew" preserved over LOGOS's "refashioned." The Greek ἀνακτίζεσθαι = to be rebuilt/refashioned. Both are accurate; LOGOS's "refashioned" and EMET's "fashioned anew" both captured in SOPHIA's rendering.

Vv. 7–8: The description of the Red Sea crossing is deliberately understated — a list of transformations. PNEUMA elaborates; LOGOS and EMET stay close to the Greek.

V. 13: The comparison of Egyptian sin with Sodomite sin: LOGOS renders this most clearly. Vv. 13–16 form a comparison: Sodom refused strangers (bad) — Egypt welcomed then enslaved theirs (worse). PNEUMA restates this helpfully; LOGOS structure preferred.

V. 17: "the door of the righteous man" — refers to Lot (Genesis 19:11). All three agents identify the referent. "Impenetrable darkness" — all three agree.

V. 18: The harp/lyre analogy is one of the most philosophically sophisticated moments in the Deuterocanon. The argument: just as a lyre's strings produce different melodies when rearranged while preserving the same notes and rhythm, so creation's elements rearranged themselves to produce new effects while obeying the same underlying order. LOGOS's rendering is clearest and most philosophically precise. PNEUMA elaborates helpfully: "the strings are the same, the rhythm stays the same — but rearranged, they produce a completely different melody."

V. 21: "the ice-like kind of heavenly nourishment" — the manna, described as crystalline and easily dissolved (cf. Exodus 16:21, where the manna melted in the sun). All three agents agree on the identification; LOGOS's "ice-like" preserved.

V. 22: The doxological conclusion — a summary of the entire Book of History (chapters 10–19). All three agents agree substantially on the wording.
